nodes.front: Example 1 · Connect representations: For how many values of b will there be 2 solutions? 1 solution? No solution?
nodes.back: Listen for: There are an infinite number of values of b that will produce 2 solutions or no solution. There is one value of b that will produce 1 solution.

nodes.front: Example 1 · Connect representations: Suppose the constant b was added to the quadratic function instead of the linear function. For what values of b will there be 2 solutions? 1 solution? No solution?
nodes.back: Listen for: When (b<1), there are 2 solutions. When (b=1), there is one solution. When (b>1), there is no solution.

nodes.front: Example 5 · Purposeful question: How can you show that the system of equations is equivalent to the original equation?
nodes.back: Listen for: Both equations in the system are equal to y. You can substitute the second equation into the first equation to obtain the original equation.

A golfer hits toward a water hazard downhill. The hill is a line through the origin with slope -1/8; the ball's path is y = -(1/100)x^2 + (3/2)x. Part A: the hazard is 180 yd away; bounce or splash? Part B: how far from the edge of the hazard did the ball land? …

-(1/100)x^2 + (3/2)x = -(1/8)x gives x(-(1/100)x + 13/8) = 0, x = 0 or x = 162.5. Part A: bounce (162.5 < 180). Part B: 17.5 yd. Part C: yes; 180 yd along the hill is a shorter horizontal distance (about 178.6 yd), though the ball still bounces. …
Draw a rough sketch of a parabola and a line on the coordinate plane.
A. Count the number of points of intersection between the two graphs. (Sample: 2 intersections.)

B. Sketch another parabola on a coordinate plane. Use a straightedge to investigate the different ways that a line and a parabola intersect. What conjectures can you make? (No points, one point where the line is tangent, or two points.)

C. Construct Arguments: How many different numbers of intersection points are possible between a quadratic function and a linear function? Justify that you have found all of the possibilities. (Zero, one or two.)
Describe the graph you sketched. → There are two equations graphed. One is a parabola and one is a line. The parabola and the line intersect in two places.
Would using a vertical line help you determine the different number of intersection points between a linear function and a quadratic function? → No; a vertical line is not a function.

If the line is of the form y = c, would it change the number of intersection points possible, when combined with the graph of a quadratic function? → No; a horizontal line could be drawn so as not to intersect with the parabola, to only intersect it at its vertex, or to intersect it at two points.

What method did you use to determine the possible number of intersection points? → Draw a parabola. Change the position of the straight edge so that it intersects the parabola at two points, at one point, or not at all.

Does changing the position of the parabola instead of the position of the line change the number of possible intersection points from 2, 1, or 0? → No; the number of possible intersection points is the same whether you move the line or the parabola.

nodes.back: What must be true about the equation for a horizontal line that has no points of intersection with the parabola of the equation y = x^2? → The equation must be of the form y = a, for a constant a < 0.
